title: The Great Bramblehorn Bloom Race
markdown:
The tall green peaks of Bramblehorn whispered secrets on the wind: sunshine and shadows, and a special race. Elsie the young witch lived in a cozy cottage tucked amongst whispering pine trees. Her cat, Pip, was very proud, as black as a starless night, emerald eyes always seeming to judge his naps. He was very sure his whiskers were the most wonderful in all of Bramblehorn, longer and fancier than any other cat’s.

The annual Bramblehorn Blossom Race was about to begin. Not a race for speed. A race to find the very first Bramblehorn Blossom, blooming for just one day, high on the mountain, petals shimmering like captured starlight. This year Elsie was excited. She’d heard that young Albie, a wizard who could turn pebbles into puddles and make his owl Flicker do somersaults, was also competing. Their rivalry was as warm and bubbly as a fizzy potion, always ending in good spirits.

“Are we ready, Pip?” Elsie asked, adjusting her pointy hat, which had a tiny winking star. Pip stretched lazily. His tail gave a flick that could have knocked a teacup off a table. “As ready as I’ll ever be for more human silliness,” he purred, but his emerald eyes held a glint of excitement. He particularly enjoyed chasing butterflies that flitted just out of reach.

They set off. Crisp air, pine needles, damp earth from a recent shower. The path wound upwards past gnarled trees like sleeping giants and mossy rocks cool and smooth beneath Elsie’s fingertips. She hummed a cheerful bouncy tune that made Pip’s whiskers twitch. Broomstick under her arm, bristles tickling her elbow. Pip trotted beside her, nose twitching: faint sweetness of wild thyme, sharp tang of crushed fern, the intriguing scent of a badger’s home.

Soon a patch of bouncy toadstools, plump and red with white polka dots. Elsie giggled, testing one with her boot. It wobbled and sprang back with a satisfying boing. Albie, just ahead, was trying to hop across, robes flapping. Flicker, the tiny owl, perched on his shoulder, head swivelling like a miniature periscope.

“Careful, Albie. You might bounce right into the clouds.”

Albie, mid-hop, wobbled. “These things have a mind of their own. They’re trying to tickle my toes.” He landed with a thump in a soft heap of fallen leaves. Flicker hooted softly, a gentle sigh, as if to say: patience. The mountain has many lessons.

Elsie and Pip were more interested in a family of giggling gnomes carefully polishing dewdrops on spiderwebs, tiny chandeliers. Sparkling like diamonds. Laughter like a hundred tiny silver bells. Pip forgot the race for a moment, amazed by a fat bumblebee buzzing lazily past plump ruby-red wild strawberries. He crouched low, not to hunt, to admire fuzzy determined flight and sunlight on tiny wings. Head tilted. Whiskers quivering.

Elsie sat on soft velvety moss that felt like sleeping on a cloud. Sunlight through tall pines, dancing patterns of light and shadow. Gentle buzz of insects. A clear bubbling stream in the distance. A moment to just be. Tiny hairs on a fern frond seemed to glow. A ladybug, shiny red shell and perfect black dots, climbed a blade of grass as if climbing a mountain. The world seemed to hold its breath. She remembered her grandmother saying nature always offered the best kind of magic.

Meanwhile Albie had found a herd of very friendly, very silly mountain goats trying to play leapfrog over a fallen log. Beards bounced. Hooves scrambled. Bleats of delight. Flicker watched from a nearby branch with quiet amusement. Albie squared his shoulders, took a deep breath, tried to leap. Long wizard robes caught on a snag. He tumbled head over heels into a patch of soft sweet-smelling clover. Flicker hooted a little laugh, dry leaves.

Later, as the sun dipped, orange, rose, lavender, Elsie and Pip rejoined the main path and saw Albie and Flicker ahead, not rushing, pointing and chattering, voices on the evening breeze.

“Look, Elsie.” Albie waved, robes a bit grass-stained. “The most amazing glow-worms. A whole constellation on that rock. Like a little piece of the night sky came down to visit.”

They hurried over. Hundreds of tiny glow-worms blinking together on a dark ancient boulder, a magical starlit pattern pulsing with gentle light. Breathtaking.

“Wow.” Elsie’s eyes wide. “I’ve never seen so many together.”

Pip seemed to have forgotten pride and race. He sat and watched, emerald eyes reflecting the glow, a soft happy rumble.

Albie smiled, big and happy. “I suppose we got a little distracted.”

Elsie nodded. Warm as hot chocolate on a chilly evening. “We certainly did. But it was such fun. I saw a woodpecker trying to build a nest upside down.”

“And Flicker tried to teach a squirrel how to whistle. The squirrel just chattered back, very annoyed.”

They burst into laughter, a cascade through twilight-dusted trees. The Blossom race was forgotten. They did not need to name the prize. They walked back down side by side, Pip a velvety shadow, Flicker fluttering near Albie. The trees rustled. The first Bramblehorn Blossom, somewhere high, could bloom for its one day without them. Pip’s whiskers, if they were the finest in Bramblehorn, did not mind, which was how you knew a race could lose its hurry and still count as won.
characters: Elsie (young witch of Bramblehorn), Pip (a proud black cat with emerald eyes)
author: StoryGen Community
